rotation.topic: Bypassing Safety Controls · Stop Work Authority

openingMessage: The process is about what you need to do today, in practice, in the film room, in the weight room, so that you can be the best player you can be.
openingWhy: Our film room is seven hundred OWL forms of what the field actually did. Our weight room is the morning cal, the LMRA, the trailer check. Champions in this trade are built in the same boring rooms as champions anywhere — daily, unglamorous, non-negotiable.
leadershipThought: Character is built when nobody is watching. Small deviations don't stay small. Correct them now, when the cost is low.

specialFocus.title: Stop Work, Written Down — Recreate the Location in Words
specialFocus.why: Jacob's week — Bypassing Safety Controls · Stop Work Authority — launches TODAY, Monday, and it starts with a look back at last week. This crew filed 533 forms last week. 'Stop work authority was discussed' was ticked on nearly every one. 'Stop work authority UTILIZED' was ticked ZERO times. Yet buried in the notes are at least 13 real stops — a pipe rigged wrong, a valve leaking by, a casing leak, lightning call-offs, a mask-up on benzene, a sensor shut off — most living in a single line nobody could rebuild later. We ARE making the calls. We are NOT writing them so anyone else can see them. This week we close that gap. The habit is two moves, every time: make the call, then paint the scene. A safety professional's notes should let anyone — a client, a superintendent, the office, the next crew — see the location the way you saw it: the wellhead, the wind, the readings, where the crew stood, and why you made the decision you made. That's what protects us as a team when someone asks 'why did you stop work?' — we don't argue, we hand them the day. When this topic ran in cycle one (Meeting Log, week 8) the lesson was: a bypass nobody writes down is a bypass the next hand never knew existed. This week's version: a stop nobody writes down never happened. Monday opens with last week's stops below; after that, one scenario a day — Jacob picks.
specialFocus.standardLabel: Make the Call, Then Paint the Scene
standard: Anyone can stop, and everyone backs it. Stop work belongs to every hand on the location — ours or theirs, 1099 or twenty-year man. Nobody gets second-guessed for stopping in good faith. The only wrong stop is the one you didn't call.

Stop means STOP: make it safe, get people out of the line of fire, THEN talk. Never 'let me just finish this one thing.' And the restart is a decision too — what changed, readings back where they belong, and who cleared it.

Never bypass to keep moving. A monitor you silence, a sensor you switch off, a barrier you step over, a step you skip — that IS bypassing a safety control. If a device has to come out of service, your lead hears it right then, something else covers that area, and it goes in the notes with the time and the reason.

Write the scene in six parts — and tick 'Stop work authority utilized': WHERE (exact location name, job number) · WHEN (time stopped, time resumed) · WHAT YOU SAW (readings with numbers, wind direction, weather, what changed) · WHO (who called it, who you told, when) · WHAT YOU DID (pulled back, masked up, mustered, moved trucks, called parts) · HOW IT ENDED (what fixed it, who cleared the restart, or why it was called off).

Add color to your decisions. A client will question the decision, so the note has to carry the reasoning: why you masked up instead of pulling back, why the trucks went to the north side, why ten minutes of watching the sky turned into a call-off. Write it so someone who was never there could draw the location from your words.

'Who was told' is never blank. Name the company man, the MT, or your lead — and the time. A problem you found but didn't report is a problem nobody else knows exists, and a stop the customer never heard about from us is a stop they'll hear about from somebody else first.

scenarios.title: Monday Opener — Last Week's Stops (10/12–10/18)
scenarios.body: Close out last week first: Hot Work with Ray hosting, and every morning carried a habit that doesn't expire — the JSA signed by crew AND company man before work on an active gas well, a full 360 and gauged tires before every roll, every job and pivot called in by exact location name, cool heads when it gets hot, spoken handoffs on every relief. Now the stops, and they were good calls: Humberto Marquez-Salazar stopped the job at McClintic A 8H because the pipe wasn't rigged up right — his partner Jeremy Norris wrote it up as 'a great use of stop work authority.' Baldemar Bracamontes caught a valve leaking by on the bleeder pretest at Frank 11E 105H — stopped, huddled, fixed, then went. Luis Zarate watched the lightning on Nobles, then called University 7-43 74H off when it struck too close. Bryan Medlin put the crew under SCBA at 10 ppm benzene on NUNN 14 TK554. Ralph Forbes held the manlift work for wind. Larry Jaramillo got a broken-handle hammer out of a crew's hands. That's Stop Work Authority working. The gap: not one was logged as 'utilized,' and most are one line. Medlin's — a reading, a wind direction, the action — was the best note of the week, and it still left out the time and who was told. Starting today, every stop gets the six-part scene.

scenarios.title: The Stop That Disappeared
scenarios.body: This one is ours, from Wednesday. The pipe wasn't rigged up right, Humberto stopped the job, the crew fixed it, and the disconnect finished clean — textbook. Now jump six weeks. The operator's office calls: why did the crew lose time on McClintic A 8H on 10/14? The form says one line. Nobody remembers the time, what exactly was wrong, or who on location was told. A great call just became a he-said-she-said. Rebuild it as a circle, out loud: '07:40, McClintic A 8H, disconnect. Line was rigged ___. I called stop because ___. Told the company man, ___, at ___. Rig crew re-rigged with ___. Restart cleared at ___ by ___.' Same stop — but now it ends the conversation in one email instead of starting an argument.

scenarios.title: The Valve That Leaked By — Read It, It's the Template
scenarios.body: From last week, written by Baldemar Bracamontes at Frank 11E 105H: 'Had pre task meeting, when we started our pretest on bleeders we noticed a valve was leaking by, stopped and got together to discuss next steps, after valves were fixed continued without further incidents.' Read it out loud. You can see it: the pretest, the leak-by, the stop, the huddle, the fix, the restart. That's the backbone of a great stop note. Now add the three things that make it bulletproof — the time, who on location was told, and who cleared the restart — and it's a note that ends any conversation before it starts. Circle drill: take your last job and write it in that same shape, right now.

scenarios.title: The Sensor Switched Off at Midnight
scenarios.body: Night shift on a rig, this past week: the element on an LEL sensor at the shakers looked damaged, so it got turned off. Maybe the right move — a sensor you can't trust gives false comfort. But turning it off IS taking a safety control out of service, and the shift's daily form never mentioned it. The next crew walks on with a dead spot at the shakers and no idea it's there. Rebuild it: what time it went off, which sensor, why, who was called, what covers the shakers now — a portable clipped up there? — and when the replacement is coming. A control that comes off without a note is the bypass the next hand never knew existed.

scenarios.title: Four Digits in the Wrong Box
scenarios.body: A tube pull this past week read four digits of H2S — and the only place it was written was a field meant for job accounting. No mask-up recorded, no wind, no who-was-told, no plan. Maybe everything around that reading was handled perfectly. Nobody can prove it from the paper. A number that big belongs at the top of the narrative with everything you did about it: the reading and the time, where the crew was standing and the wind, who was masked up, who you called, and what the plan became. Big readings are exactly when the paper gets read hardest — make sure yours tells the whole story.

scenarios.title: When THEIR Man Stops It
scenarios.body: Thursday: sudden rain and thunder, and the customer's MT used his stop work authority and had the whole crew cab up until it passed. Our form recorded the trigger — good — but logged only that stop work was 'discussed.' When the customer stops the job, we document it the same way we would our own: the time, who called it, the conditions, how long the crew sat, what the restart criteria were, and who gave the go. Their stop is still our day — and if the invoice or the schedule gets questioned later, our notes should match theirs line for line.

scenarios.title: The Email Six Weeks Later
scenarios.body: Make-believe, but it happens: the superintendent's email lands — 'Your crew sat on our location for forty minutes last month. Explain.' Two techs could have worked that job. Tech one's form says 'stopped job, unsafe conditions.' Tech two's says '9:12 — benzene 10 ppm at the break, wind out of the south, crew under SCBA, told the company man at 9:14, readings back to zero at 9:40, restart cleared by him at 9:52.' Read both out loud. One starts a fight; the other ends it in a single reply. Same stop, same decision — the only difference is what got written down.

scenarios.title: Lightning Was Too Close — How Close?
scenarios.body: Luis did it right on Wednesday: watched the storm on one job, then called the next one off when the strikes came in too close and weren't letting up. Now read it like a client would. 'Too close' — how close? What time did it start, who made the call, did the company man agree, when did the crew leave, was it rescheduled? Every one of those answers existed on location for about ten minutes. Write it while it's real: 'Strikes inside ___ miles at ___, crew to the trucks at ___, called off at ___ with ___ agreeing, rescheduled for ___.' Weather calls are the stops most likely to be second-guessed later — because by then the sky is clear.

questions: Last week you made a call that changed the job — a pause, a mask-up, a reschedule. Say your write-up out loud: where, when, what you saw, who you told, what you did, how it ended. What part did you have to guess at?
We stopped at least 13 times last week and ticked 'Stop work authority utilized' zero times. Why don't we count our own stops?
Where's the line between 'pausing to fix something' and 'stopping work' — and why should both get written down?
Has a safety device ever come off on your location — a sensor out, a monitor silenced, a barrier moved? Who knew, and what covered for it?
What makes a note good enough that a client could picture the location? Give one detail you'll add from now on that you usually leave out.
Jacob's question: what did the field teach us yesterday that the breakroom should know?
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: Stop it, make it safe, then write the scene: where, when, what you saw with numbers, who you told, what you did, and how it ended. No bypass to keep the job moving, and no stop goes unwritten. Our notes are how we prove the call was right.
